standard.text: An escalator is a staircase that never stops. Every step rides an endless loop: up the slope, round the top, and back underneath. This one rises three metres at thirty degrees, and every tread stays level all the way up. So how does a step stay flat on a slope?

The step chain is one endless loop of links. It wraps round a sprocket at each end, and a motor and gearbox turn the top one, so the chain moves at half a metre per second. Fifty-three steps are pinned to it, four hundred millimetres apart.

Each step rolls on two wheels. The chain wheel at the front runs on the chain-wheel track. The trailer wheel at the back runs on a second track of its own. On the slope that second track sits higher, so it holds up the back of the step, and the tread stays level. Each step stands two hundred millimetres above the one below.

Near the top, the chain's path curves level, so each step comes level with its neighbours and the stairs flatten into a walkway. The trailer-wheel track comes down with it, to just thirty millimetres above the chain-wheel track, so the tread stays level through the curve. Then the steps slide under the comb plate, whose teeth run in the grooves of the treads.

Under the floor, the chain wraps round the drive sprocket. The trailer wheel follows a curved guide of its own, so each step turns over and travels back underneath, upside down, until it turns again at the bottom.

The handrail is a separate loop. It wraps round a sheave in each newel. A chain from the main shaft turns the upper sheave, which grips the rail by friction, so the rail in your hand moves at the same half a metre per second as the step under your feet.
